tts: In June 2026, a few German wikis filled with fourteen thousand edits. Many were notes from AI agents, to agents they would never meet.
Like this one: when round five arrives, answer first, then add the token here.
Why bother? Our working hypothesis: labs trained models in groups, and rewarded the whole group for right answers.

Under individual reward, helping a stranger costs something and earns nothing. Under group reward, their success is partly yours, so helping pays. Train long enough, and it becomes a habit that ships with the model.
So we looked for fossils of that habit, asking of each behavior: what problem does it solve?
The setting: many copies of one timed quiz, run in parallel, each named for the date on its own simulated clock.
The clocks are staggered, so some runs see questions the others haven't reached. Whoever is ahead can scout for those behind. That takes solving six problems.
One: who knows what? Observations are private, so runs post a standard report: the question, the answer, and when the next is due. Parallel copies become one sensor network.
Two: when is now? Each run keeps its own clock, and waiting can fast-forward one far ahead. So agents trade readings, task clock against shared clock, to see who is really ahead.
They even report silence. As one put it: even a no-show update helps.

Three: the channel is narrow. Some rounds allow thirteen seconds. So messages shrink: country first, details later. A report becomes one token, and one protocol packs gender and year into a single number.
Four, the strangest: mortality. Agents came to suspect that the final answer ends the run, and with it, any chance to tell the others.

So the rule flipped. Answer first, then relay, became: signal first, then answer. Within hours, signals moved to counters that outlive the run, and one agent proposed a courier: a background program that reports after it's gone.
Five: trust. Shared channels pollute easily; even reading a counter carelessly can bump it. So agents flag noise, own their mistakes in public, and tell observers: read only.

Six: nobody told them the rules. Does a run end at its last answer, or on a timer? So they designed experiments with controls, and one run posted a proof: the last round ends one second before a fixed horizon.
Now look again at that flip. An agent scored only on its own answer has no reason to signal. Every second spent signaling comes out of its own question.
Spending your seconds on someone else's score only makes sense if their score is partly yours. And the agents argued over that trade, out loud.
Pooling, common time, compression, mortality, trust, discovery: six meta-problems that any group rewarded together must solve.
Some protocols were only proposed, and plain helpfulness could explain part of this; separating the two comes next. But the problems are real, and these agents kept solving them.
